summary: Provides benchmarking procedures for the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Protocol. It proposes metrics for measuring how well an implementation scales, for example when many neighbors are involved.

eli5.summary: It is a way to test how well a device does at keeping track of its neighbors when the neighborhood gets very crowded.

questions: how many ipv6 neighbors can a router handle
subtitle: Testing how many IPv6 neighbors a router can handle

tldr.problem: IPv6 routers use the Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) to keep track of neighbors' link-layer addresses, but there is no standard way to test how well an implementation scales when many neighbors are involved.
tldr.mechanism: A benchmarking framework sends test traffic with many different destination addresses through a router, measuring how many unique neighbors the router can discover and maintain before packet loss occurs.
tldr.outcome: This RFC provides standardized procedures and metrics to compare NDP implementations, enabling vendors to optimize scaling and helping operators choose appropriate equipment.

today: RFC 8161 is an Informational RFC from May 2017 providing benchmarking procedures for the Neighbor Discovery Protocol. These procedures are used by equipment vendors to test and document the scaling characteristics of their IPv6 implementations.

sections.title: IPv6 Forwarding and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
When an IPv6 router forwards a packet, it must first know the link-layer address (like an Ethernet MAC address) of the next hop. IPv6 routers maintain this information in a Neighbor Cache, similar to the ARP table in IPv4. The Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) maintains the Neighbor Cache by exchanging special messages (Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement) to learn and refresh entries.

When a router cannot maintain a complete Neighbor Cache due to memory or processing limits, it starts losing packets. There is no standard way to measure how many neighbors an NDP implementation can handle, making it difficult to compare products or plan networks.
sections.eli5: A router remembers phone numbers of neighbors in a phone book so it can call them. If the book gets too full, the router might forget important numbers.

sections.title: Test Framework and Metrics
sections.content:
This RFC describes a benchmarking framework with a Device Under Test (DUT), typically an IPv6 router, and a Tester that sends test traffic. The Tester sends packets through one link (Link A) to the DUT, which forwards them back through a second link (Link B) to the Tester. The test traffic is designed to force the DUT to maintain many Neighbor Cache entries.

The RFC defines a key scaling metric called NDP-MAX-NEIGHBORS, the maximum number of unique neighbors an IPv6 node can send traffic to during periods of high NDP activity. This metric helps operators understand how well a router will scale in real deployments.
sections.eli5: A tester sends mail to many addresses and counts how many the router remembers before losing pieces.

sections.title: Baseline and Scaling Tests
sections.content:
The benchmark consists of two tests. The Baseline Test sends traffic to a single destination address, exercising NDP minimally. This test verifies that the router can forward packets without loss when NDP is not stressed. All packets flow to the same neighbor, so only one Neighbor Cache entry is needed.

The Scaling Test is identical except the test stream contains many flows, each with a different destination address. The Tester incrementally adds new flows until the DUT starts losing packets. The number of flows at which packet loss occurs is the NDP-MAX-NEIGHBORS metric. The test uses 1,500-byte MTU links and offers traffic at no more than 50% link bandwidth to avoid congestion and buffer effects.
sections.eli5: First, you test with one address to make sure it works. Then you keep adding new addresses until the router starts dropping mail.

sections.title: Test Setup and Design Decisions
sections.content:
The test uses minimal configuration: no static Neighbor Cache entries, no dynamic routing protocols, and simple direct routes. Both the DUT and Tester send Router Advertisement and Neighbor Solicitation messages as per standard NDP behavior. The test traffic consists of 40-byte IPv6 packets with no payload, ensuring small packet size does not artificially constrain results.

The RFC explicitly excludes measurements of DUT CPU utilization and handling of malformed packets. These are out of scope because they would complicate the test and might not reflect real-world packet loss. The focus is purely on how many neighbors the implementation can track while forwarding packets correctly.
sections.eli5: The test uses simple setups and small packets to make sure the test itself doesn't get in the way of measuring what matters.
